evidence.text:
Title: Patient Contrastive Learning: a Performant, Expressive, and Practical Approach to ECG Modeling.
Abstract: Supervised machine learning applications in health care are often limited due to a scarcity of labeled training data. To mitigate this effect small sample size, we introduce pre-training approach, Patient Contrastive Learning Representations (PCLR), which creates latent representations ECGs from large number unlabeled examples. The resulting expressive, performant, and practical across wide spectrum clinical tasks. We develop PCLR using system with over 3.2 million 12-lead ECGs, demonstrate substantial improvements multiple new tasks when there fewer than 5,000 labels.

Title: Screening for cardiac contractile dysfunction using an artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiogram
Abstract: Asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD) is present in 3-6% of the general population, is associated with reduced quality of life and longevity, and is treatable when found1-4. An inexpensive, noninvasive screening tool for ALVD in the doctor's office is not available. We tested the hypothesis that application of artificial intelligence (AI) to the electrocardiogram (ECG), a routine method of measuring the heart's electrical activity, could identify ALVD. Using paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram data, including the left ventricular ejection fraction (a measure of contractile function), from 44,959 patients at the Mayo Clinic, we trained a convolutional neural network to identify patients with ventricular dysfunction, defined as ejection fraction ≤35%, using the ECG data alone. When tested on an independent set of 52,870 patients, the network model yielded values for the area under the curve, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 0.93, 86.3%, 85.7%, and 85.7%, respectively. In patients without ventricular dysfunction, those with a positive AI screen were at 4 times the risk (hazard ratio, 4.1; 95% confidence interval, 3.3 to 5.0) of developing future ventricular dysfunction compared with those with a negative screen. Application of AI to the ECG-a ubiquitous, low-cost test-permits the ECG to serve as a powerful screening tool in asymptomatic individuals to identify ALVD.

gold.abstract: Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are an established technique to screen for abnormal cardiac signals. Recent work has established that it is possible to detect arrhythmia directly from the ECG signal using deep learning algorithms. While a few prior approaches with contrastive learning have been successful, the best way to define a positive sample remains an open question. In this project, we investigate several ways to define positive samples, and assess which approach yields the best performance in a downstream task of classifying arrhythmia. We explore spatiotemporal invariances, generic augmentations, demographic similarities, cardiac rhythms, and wave attributes of ECG as potential ways to match positive samples. We then evaluate each strategy with downstream task performance, and find that learned representations invariant to patient identity are powerful in arrhythmia detection. We made our code available in: https://github.com/mandiehyewon/goodviews_ecg.git

--- Researcher B ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b: PCLR provides a self-supervised contrastive pre-training method that learns ECG representations from 3.2 million unlabeled 12-lead ECGs and improves downstream clinical tasks with fewer than 5,000 labels.
- Paper-c: Demonstrates a supervised CNN using paired ECG-echocardiogram data can screen asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD; ejection fraction ≤35%) with AUC 0.93, and a positive AI screen predicts future ventricular dysfunction.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use PCLR’s pre-trained ECG encoder as the feature extractor for the ALVD screening task from paper-c. Contrastive pre-training supplies a rich, label-efficient representation; paper-c supplies the clinically validated outcome definition and screening framework. The operational connection is fine-tuning PCLR on small labeled ECG-echocardiogram pairs. Missing cross-paper knowledge: PCLR was not evaluated for ALVD or echo-derived ejection fraction, and paper-c did not use self-supervised pre-training; whether PCLR embeddings retain contractile-dysfunction information is unknown.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Obtain an external cohort with paired 12-lead ECGs and echocardiograms. Pre-train PCLR on unlabeled ECGs from the same institution, then fine-tune for EF≤35 using only 500, 1,000, and 5,000 labeled ECG-echo pairs. Compare against a from-scratch CNN matching paper-c and a linear probe on frozen PCLR features. Measure AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and calibration on held-out echo labels; additionally follow screen-positive patients without baseline dysfunction to estimate hazard ratio for incident ALVD. Validate across at least two sites.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We integrate self-supervised ECG representation learning with echocardiogram-defined ALVD screening to reduce labeled-data requirements. PCLR representations are fine-tuned on small ECG-echo cohorts and benchmarked against a supervised CNN. The study tests whether contrastive pre-training preserves contractile-dysfunction signals and improves low-label screening performance, enabling scalable ALVD detection with limited echo labels.

FINAL IDEA: Fine-tuning PCLR’s contrastively pre-trained ECG representations on small ECG-echocardiogram cohorts can make paper-c’s ALVD screening more label-efficient and broadly deployable.

--- Researcher C ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
Paper-b: PCLR learns latent 12-lead ECG representations via contrastive pre-training on 3.2 million unlabeled ECGs and improves downstream clinical tasks with fewer than 5,000 labels.
Paper-c: A supervised CNN trained on 44,959 paired ECG-echocardiograms detects asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF ≤35%) from ECG alone, reporting AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%, and a 4.1 hazard ratio for future dysfunction.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use PCLR’s self-supervised ECG encoder as a frozen feature extractor or fine-tuned initialization for a lightweight ALVD classifier. The operational link is transfer of unlabeled ECG representations to reduce the number of expensive paired echocardiogram labels needed for contractile-dysfunction screening.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Cohort: de-identified 12-lead ECGs with paired echocardiograms and LVEF. Train PCLR encoder + linear/logistic head on small labeled sets of 500, 1,000, 2,500, and 5,000 patients. Baseline: de novo CNN from paper-c trained on the same small sets; linear probe of PCLR. Compare against paper-c’s reported fully supervised performance.

Using PCLR with small ECG-echo training sets, we will evaluate noninferiority to a fully supervised CNN trained on 44,959 pairs. This could extend low-label ECG modeling to structural/functional cardiac screening and clarify whether contrastive ECG features transfer to LVEF prediction.

FINAL IDEA: Integrating PCLR self-supervised ECG pretraining with supervised ECG-echocardiogram screening to test whether contrastive ECG representations enable accurate detection of asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction with far fewer labeled echocardiograms than a de novo CNN.
